title: Checkpoint 0: Stockfish (skill 0) vs Magnus
notes: Checkpoint after game 0, from the Queen's Gambit Declined: Magnus plays the yardstick, Stockfish at skill 0. Nothing is studied afterwards.

moves.thought: I checked 5...dxc4, but 6.Qxb7 forks a8/b8 and after 6...Nbd7 7.Qxa8 I simply lose a rook, so the pawn grab fails. Instead 5...c6 is solid: it reinforces d5, keeps b7 covered by the bishop, and prepares a later dxc4 followed by b5 to hit the queen with tempo.

The position is a solid Semi-Slav/QGD structure where my king needs safety before White can exploit the g5-bishop and the Qb3/c4 pressure on d5. Castling develops safely and prepares Nbd7 without allowing annoying pins like Bb5 after an exchange on d5.

Bxa3 simply loses a piece to bxa3, so I ignore that bait; instead I complete development with Nbd7, keeping a solid Orthodox QGD structure and preparing dxc4 with b5 or a central ...e5 later. I checked that cxd5 exd5 and Bxf6 Nxf6 leave nothing for White, since Nxd5 is met by cxd5 winning a piece.

I want to resolve the pressure from Bg5 before committing in the centre; 8...h6 either wins the bishop pair after Bxf6 Nxf6 or gains a tempo if the bishop retreats to h4, after which dxc4 followed by b5 and c5 is available. I checked that nothing is loose — no captures or checks for White create problems, since my king is safe and d5 is adequately defended.

I must recapture on f6, and Nxf6 is the best version: the knight gets an active square while the bishop stays on e7 (if I play Bxf6 or gxf6 my knight stays passive on d7, and Qb6 would simply drop the e7 bishop to Bxe7). I checked 10.Qxb7 Rb8 11.Qa6 Rxb2, where I regain the pawn with an active rook, and 10.cxd5 can be met by Nxd5 or exd5, so the b7 pawn is not a real problem.

White's knight on e5 is the only active piece, so I challenge it immediately with Nd7, keeping my structure intact; after Nxd7 Bxd7 or Nf3 I'm solid. I checked the tactic 11.Nxc6 bxc6 12.Qxc6 — my knight on d7 is covered twice by queen and bishop, and after Rb8 White has only two pawns for a piece.

White's knight retreat gave me time to improve; I want to resolve the center tension favourably rather than release it with dxc4 (which frees White's position). Nb6 develops the knight to an active square, adds a second attacker to c4, and keeps b7 safe since Qxb7 loses to Bxb7; if White pushes c5 then Nc4 is an excellent outpost, and cxd5 just gives me easy equality.

White's a4 threatens a5 to kick my b6 knight, and both a4 and c4 are guarded by the queen so Nxa4/Nxc4 just lose a piece. I played a5 to stop the pawn advance, keeping my knight secure on b6 while retaining the solid d5/e6/c6 structure; if White tries c5 I retreat with Nd7 and undermine with b6.

Nxa4 loses a piece since the queen on b3 guards a4, so I resolved the central tension instead: after 13...dxc4 14.Bxc4 Nxc4 15.Qxc4 I trade my knight for White's light-squared bishop, keeping the bishop pair, and I can then free myself with ...c5. Material stays level and I get a comfortable, symmetrical game.

White's Qa2 hits my extra c4 pawn along the a2–g8 diagonal, and I can't defend it (b7–b5 is blocked by my own knight, and Qd5 drops the queen to Nxd5), so I prefer the active Nd5, which is securely covered by the queen, e6 and c6 pawns. If White trades with Nxd5 then exd5 finally protects c4 and I keep my extra pawn; if he plays e4, Nxc3 bxc3 followed by b5 also holds c4, and Bxc4/Qxc4 only regains the pawn while I gain time and the bishop pair.

My d5 knight is safe (defended twice by the c6 and e6 pawns), but 15...b5 at once fails to 16.axb5 cxb5 17.Nxd5 exd5 18.Bxd5 winning material, and 15...Nb6 achieves little since a4 is guarded by both Qa2 and Ra1. So I trade on c3 first, giving White doubled c-pawns and preparing ...b5 with tempo against the c4 bishop followed by ...Bb7 and queenside play.

My knight on c3 is hit twice (Qb3 and the b2 pawn), so it must move; Nd5 retreats to the strongest square, where it is defended twice by the e6 and c6 pawns, and if Bxd5 I simply recapture with a pawn keeping a solid structure and the bishop pair. Nxa4 just loses the knight to Qxa4, and Nb5 Bxb5 cxb5 drops the b-pawn to Qxb5.

White's Qb3 and Bc4 both bear down on my queenside, and I calculated that 17...c5 loses a pawn to 18.Bxd5 exd5 19.Qxd5, while 17...b5 18.axb5 cxb5 19.Bxb5 just drops a pawn since b5 would be undefended, and 17...b6 is simply met by Qxb6. So I play 17...Rb8, which guards b7 along the file (freeing my c8 bishop later) and properly prepares ...b5 with the rook supporting the b-pawn.

White's e4 attacks my undefended knight on d5, so I must move it; Nc3 and Ne3 simply lose a piece, and Nf6 invites e5 with tempo gain. Nb6 retreats while hitting the Bc4, gaining time to follow up with c5 or Bb7 against White's big centre.

White's queen just captured my knight on b6, but b6 is undefended — the bishop on c4, knight on f3, and b2 pawn all fail to cover it, so my queen on d8 can recapture along the d8-c7-b6 diagonal. That nets a queen for a knight, and White has no check or discovery in reply (Bxe6 is simply met by fxe6).

I'm up a queen for a knight, so I just need safe material and no tactics; Qxd4 loses the queen to Nxd4, but b2 is completely undefended (neither rook nor bishop covers it) so Qxb2 wins a clean pawn, and after Rab1 my queen simply steps to a3 or c3 with no trap.

My queen on b2 is attacked by Rab1 and undefended, and the tempting captures all lose it (Qxb1 Rxb1, Qxd4 Nxd4, Qxf2+ Rxf2, Qc2/Qe2 Bxc2/Bxe2, Qd2 Nxd2, Qc1/Qa1 Rxc1/Rxa1, and every b-file square drops to Rxb-something). Qa3 is a safe square untouched by the rooks, bishop and knight, and it also attacks the loose a4 pawn, gaining a tempo while I keep my extra pawn and bishop pair.

White's Ra1 attacks my queen, but it also abandoned the b1-rook's guard duty — the bishop on d3 is now completely undefended (no rook or knight covers it). Qxd3 saves the queen from the rook's attack and wins a whole piece; I verified Nf3 and Rf1 do not cover d3 and there's no discovered counterattack.

My queen on d3 is attacked by the knight, and I'm already up a queen and bishop for a knight, so I just need a safe square that keeps the material. Qxd4 runs into Nxc6 forking queen, bishop and rook, but Qxe4 grabs a pawn safely — Nxc6 there is simply met by bxc6, and Nxf7 by Rxf7.

My queen on e4 is attacked by the rook on e1, so I must move it, and Qxd4 both saves the queen and grabs the pawn while leaving the e5 knight undefended (Rd1 then loses it to Qxe5). I checked White's tries: Nxc6 bxc6 just drops the knight, Nf3 or Nd7 (Bxd7) cost White nothing but gain nothing, and I remain up a queen and bishop for a knight.

White's knight on g6 forks my bishop on e7 and rook on f8, so I simply capture it; after 25...fxg6 the rook lift 26.Rxe6 fails to 26...Bxe6 since my c8 bishop covers e6 through d7, and 26.Rxf8+ Bxf8 is just a trade. That leaves me a clean piece up with queen, two rooks and two bishops against two rooks.

I'm up a queen and two bishops for nothing, so I just need safety and simplification — Qxf2+ and Rxf2 both invite recaptures that needlessly trade my winning material (after Rxf2 Rxf2 the queen capture on f2 is met by Kxf2). Qxa4 snatches a free pawn while b7 stays defended by my rook and White has no checks or threats at all.

My queen on a4 is attacked by the rook on a1, and while Qxa1 wins a rook, it trades my queen for it; instead I keep the queen, since Q+2R+2B against two rooks is overwhelming. Qd4 centralizes, hits f2, and is completely safe — White has no checks or captures in reply.

I'm up a queen and two bishops for nothing, so the safest path is simplification rather than a flashy sacrifice — Qxf2+ would just trade my queen for a rook since f2 is doubly defended. Rf5 offers a rook trade along the fifth rank (Rxf5 gxf5 leaves me Q+R+2B vs a lone rook), and if White declines, I still have Rxf2 followed by Qxf2+ winning material again.

I'm far ahead in material (Q+2R+2B vs 2R), so I want forcing simplification that keeps my queen. Rxf2 is protected by my queen on d4, and if White takes with Rxf2 then Qxf2+ Kh1 Qxa2 scoops the other rook along the second rank; otherwise White's f1-rook is simply attacked and overloaded.

I'm massively ahead in material (Q + R + 2B + 6 pawns vs 2R + 2 pawns), so I just want a safe forcing move that stops White's ideas of Rf7 hitting my bishop and g7. Qd1+ is a clean check: Rf1 or Ra1 interpositions just lose the rook to Qxf1+/Qxa1+ while leaving me a winning endgame, so White must play Kh2, after which I consolidate with Bd6+ or Kh7.

I'm up a queen and two bishops for a rook, so I just need safe, forcing play: Bc5 activates the bishop on the long diagonal toward f2, immediately pressuring the f2 rook while keeping my queen flexible to pile on with Qd4 next. I checked White's only tricks, Rf8+ and Ra8, and both just lose a rook (Kxf8 / Rxa8).

My queen on d1 is attacked by Rd2 (defended by Rf2), so Qxd2 or Bxf2 would just trade my queen for a rook; I also checked that Qc2, Qe2, Qf1, Qf3, Qg1+ and Qh1+ all simply lose the queen to a rook or the king. Qc1 is a safe retreat where neither rook can reach me (Rd1 or Rc2 would drop a rook to Qxd1/Qxc1), and with queen, rook and two bishops versus two rooks I only need to keep everything protected.

Only two legal replies to the check; Bf8 just drops the bishop for a rook after Rxf8+, while Kh7 keeps my extra material — if White grabs the bishop with Rxc8 I recapture Rxc8, trading his rook for my bishop and leaving me with queen, rook and bishop against a lone rook. No White mating threats exist after Kh7 since my queen covers the dark squares and the h-file is safe.

White's doubled rooks on the eighth rank have no mate (Rh8+ just loses to Kxh8), and my bishop on c5 can simply take the rook on f8 since c8 is already guarded by Rb8. After Bxf8 Rxf8 (or Rxc8 Rxc8) I am up a full rook with queen and bishop still active, which is completely winning.

White's rook on d8 is undefended and currently attacks my bishop on c8, so I need to meet that threat; Be7 attacks the rook while also meaning that Rxc8 is answered by Rxc8, winning a rook. I checked White has no checks or counter-tactics after Be7, so I keep my huge material lead and consolidate.

White's rook on d8 is completely undefended and my bishop on e7 attacks it, so I simply win a whole rook, leaving White with only king and two pawns against my queen, rook, two bishops and pawns. I checked that White has no checks or counterthreats after the capture.

My rook on b8 is completely blocked by my own b7 pawn, so I advance it to open the b-file — then Rb6/Rb1 combines with my queen for a quick mate (e.g. Qd2+ Kg1, Rb1#). I avoided Qf1+/Qg1+/Qh1+ since the king simply captures the queen, and White has no checks or threats at all after b5.

With queen, rook and two bishops against a bare king I just need safe forcing checks that never put my queen next to the king — Qe3+, Qf1+ and Qg1+ would all simply be captured. Qf4+ checks down the f-file from a safe distance, covering f1/f2/f3 and e3/g3/d2, driving the king toward the edge where I can bring Bh4+ and the rook in for mate.

White is down to king and two pawns, so I only need to avoid blunders: Qxg4 loses the queen to hxg4, and Qf2+/Qf3+/Qg3+/Qf1+/Qh2+ all put the queen on a square adjacent to Kg2 where it can simply be taken. Qe3 is safe, untouchable by the pawns, and boxes the king onto f1/g1/h1/h2 while I bring the rook and bishops over for mate.

White has only a bare king and two pawns, so I can play safely and grab material: Bxh4 wins the pawn and the bishop can't be hit, since Kg3 and Kh3 are both covered by my queen on e3. Next I'll weave a mating net with Qg3+/Qf2 ideas once the g3 square is no longer defended by the h-pawn.
The white king on f1 is boxed in, and my bishop on h4 covers f2 along the h4-g3-f2 diagonal, so Qf2 is protected and cannot be captured. That is immediate checkmate.
